messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David, a 39-year-old construction worker, presented for treatment eight months after witnessing a fatal accident on his worksite. Before the incident, he described himself as a “pretty regular guy,” proud of his work and his ability to handle the physical and mental demands of the job. That sense of normalcy was shattered the day a young apprentice, barely twenty years old, fell from the twenty-second story. David had been on the ground floor, looking up at the exact moment the scaffolding gave way. The memory of it, he reported, was not a story but a series of brutal, disjointed snapshots burned into his mind: the impossible angle of the falling body, the bloom of dust and debris on impact, the glint of the sun on a dropped tool cartwheeling through the air.

In the weeks that followed, these images began to intrude at random. The smell of wet concrete, a scent that had defined his entire working life, would suddenly transport him back, and he could taste the metallic tang of fear and dust in his mouth again, as sharp and real as it was that afternoon. The recurrence of these sensory fragments relentlessly eroded his confidence. Each time the visual of the fall flashed through his mind, it was accompanied by a paralyzing conviction of his own inadequacy; he had just stood there, a useless spectator to horror. This feeling of helplessness began to generalize, metastasizing into a core belief that he was fundamentally incapable of preventing bad things from happening, to himself or anyone else. His old worldview, one where safety protocols and hard work offered a shield against chaos, had been utterly destroyed.

This profound sense of inadequacy and the belief that the world was an uncontrollably dangerous place shaped his every waking moment. His conviction that disaster could strike at any time kept the memories on a hair trigger, ready to surface with the slightest provocation. In response to this internal torment, David developed a rigid set of coping strategies designed for one purpose: to feel nothing. He came to believe that strong emotions, especially anger at the foreman or the faulty equipment, were a dangerous indulgence he couldn't afford. He began to meticulously suppress any flicker of rage, clamping down on it until he felt a familiar, welcome numbness. When the memories became too vivid to ignore, he would resort to more drastic measures. He learned he could stare at a fixed point and deliberately try to make his mind go blank, a conscious effort to “check out” and leave his body until the wave of sensory recall had passed.

This internal battle has taken a severe toll. His ex-wife, who left six months ago, had called him a ghost, emotionally absent and unreachable. The numbness he cultivated at home was punctuated by a desperate search for distraction outside of it. Convinced of his own powerlessness, he found a fleeting sense of control and excitement in gambling. He started with small bets online, but it quickly escalated to spending entire paychecks at a local casino, chasing the thrill to drown out the intrusive images and the persistent taste of dust. The cycle has become deeply entrenched: a trigger at his new worksite—a loud bang, a young worker silhouetted against the sky—unleashes the memories. The memories reinforce his belief that he is an inadequate failure who can’t keep anyone safe. This crushing self-appraisal makes the feelings unbearable, driving him to either dissociate on the spot or to seek the oblivion of the casino later, a pattern that has left him broke and increasingly isolated. He finally sought help after a near-miss on the job, where he had zoned out while operating heavy machinery, only snapping back to reality when a coworker screamed his name. He is terrified that his inability to control his own mind will get someone else killed, a fear that is now more immediate and potent than the memories themselves.
